strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful image-editing problem with a practical interface: a source image and target emotion. Figures 1 and 6 demonstrate appealing semantic edits beyond global color or style changes.

The substantial human study provides evidence beyond classifier scores: 136 participants completed 24,480 trials, with randomized presentation and attention checks. Overall preference reaches 56% against EmoEdit and 53% against LMS.

EmoPair is a potentially useful resource, combining 331,595 emotion-labeled InstructPix2Pix pairs with 6,949 generated pairs. The manuscript attributes its underlying datasets and methods and provides a code, model, and dataset release link.

The supplement strengthens the evaluation through independently trained predictors, human-annotated emotional regions, and additional comparisons. The discussion appropriately acknowledges facial artifacts, the limitations of eight emotion categories, and possible misuse.
weaknesses: The additional architectural contribution is insufficiently established relative to iterative inference. In Table 2, the fine-tuned text-input variant improves from 5.85 to 50.24 ESMI with IEI, already approaching the complete model's 51.56. Since IEI permits up to 30 editing rounds, comparisons applying the same critic and iteration budget to competing editors, together with runtime measurements and human evaluation of this ablation, are needed to attribute the gains convincingly.

ESMI does not adequately establish the claimed preservation of structure and semantics. Its structural term, Lemo/(Lemo + Lneu + epsilon), increases when emotional-region changes grow even if neutral-region damage remains unchanged, and does not assess semantic coherence. The human study asks only which output better evokes the target emotion, without directly evaluating fidelity to the source. Consequently, an essential part of the task remains weakly validated.

The principal automatic evaluation uses the same predictor for dataset labeling, iterative selection, and emotional scoring; replacing CAM masks with human masks does not remove this dependence. CrossTest is a valuable mitigation, but agreement between ESMI and independent human judgments is still insufficiently established. Moreover, the broad superiority claims need qualification: preference against LMS falls to 47% for positive-emotion generation, and same-valence and multi-emotion generalization receive only qualitative evaluation.

Dataset quality is incompletely characterized. Approximately 98% of EmoPair consists of automatically labeled existing pairs, whereas the reported human correction concerns only 300 examples from the generated subset. No comparable audit establishes label reliability in the dominant subset, and dataset ablations do not isolate the benefits of the generated examples or subsequent human-corrected fine-tuning.

Several technical details require clarification for reproducibility. Section 3.2 defines the noised latent from the source image without clearly showing how the paired target enters diffusion training. The stated KL divergence from a predicted distribution to a one-hot target is generally infinite unless its direction or smoothing is changed. Section S2.5 omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, and sampling settings. These may be correctable reporting issues, but the implemented procedure needs to be specified; Table 1 and Table S1 also disagree on EmoEdit's ESMI, reporting 32.94 and 39.24 respectively.
